Good morning, and thank you both for coming. Before we start, three simple rules for today. First, I would like each side to tell us, in one sentence, what is non-negotiable for them. Only one thing, and only one sentence. Everything else is on the table. Second, I will ask you to make every proposal as a package, not one item at a time. The reason is simple: nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. If we close the penalty first, we will fight about the deadline for a week. And third, a word about walk-away points. Each of you should know your own very clearly. But nobody has to say it at this table, and I would recommend that you do not. Shall we begin with the operator?

I have negotiated concession contracts for thirty years, and if I could teach young lawyers only one rule, it would be this: never give anything without getting something back. Every concession is a condition. And the way you say it matters. Most people say the concession first: we can accept a penalty, if you give us more time. The problem is that the other side stops listening after the word penalty. So I always start with the condition: if you could give us more time, we would be willing to accept a penalty. Same content, very different result. And notice the verbs. While I am exploring, I say could and would, because nothing is decided yet. Only at the very end, when I am ready to close, I switch to will: if you sign today, we will deliver in year seven. Will is a promise. Do not use it too early.
